newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Krupp to forge industrial giant with Thyssen.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Krupp to forge industrial giant with Thyssen.

text.p: German industry giant Krupp confirmed on Tuesday it planned to launch a takeover bid for rival Thyssen AG, a move that would create one of the world's largest steel and engineering conglomerates.

The merger would create a steel and engineering group with annual turnover of some 63 billion marks ($37.3 billion), producing a European steel giant big enough to challenge its larger European competitors Usinor Sacilor of France and British Steel Plc and could spark further industry consolidation.
Krupp said it would offer Thyssen shareholders 435 marks a share, a 25 percent premium on Monday's closing share price, in a rare hostile takeover bid.

The announcement sparked an angry response from Thyssen, caught off guard by the unexpected grab for control of its capital, as steel workers fearing massive lay-offs downed tools in angry protest throughout the Ruhr Valley, Germany's industrial heartland.

Fried. Krupp AG Hoesch-Krupp chief Gerhard Cromme, dubbed the "job killer" after his spectacular 1991 takeover of Hoesch that resulted in over 20,000 job cuts, was booed down by steel workers at Krupp offices as he tried to explain the takeover.
Speaking behind a wall of bullet-proof riot shields under a din of shouting workers, Cromme dismissed as pure nonsense Thyssen's allegations that a takeover would cost "tens of thousands" of jobs.

"The numbers that are making the rounds are nothing but panic-mongering," he said, adding that it made sense in the interest of retaining competitive jobs in the Ruhr to forge a larger union of Germany's top two steel companies.
Cromme gave no details of the company's plans, but a Krupp spokesman later said that the Essen-based industrial titan was "fairly certain" the bid would succeed.

Around 1,000 Thyssen steel workers protested at the Krupp headquarters. Some attempted to charge the building while others threw eggs and oranges at the Krupp chairman shouting "Where is the killer?" and "Come out, Cromme!"
In Dortmund, where Krupp's steel activities are based at the former Hoesch Stahl plant, its own steel workers joined protests, fearing another round of job losses.
"Hoesch used to have three steel mills," said one woman donning blue steel worker's coveralls. "Two of them are now closed and what are young people supposed to do?"

Aside from the human cost in lost jobs -- Germany's jobless rate is the worst since 1933 -- and massive shifting of social and economic structures in the country's industrial heartland, the merger makes economic sense, analysts argue.
But Thyssen, which planned to hold a news conference in the afternoon, said it would seek to ward off Krupp advances.
"We will seek to effectively fend off this hostile takeover with partners from government and industry," Thyssen said in a statement.

But industry analysts welcomed Krupp's move on its larger rival, saying a takeover would help consolidate the German steel industry, still ailing from chronic over capacity, although they wondered how Krupp would finance the deal.
"It looks to me like a classic case where the victim gets bid up, but the value of the buyer gets called into question," said Terence Sinclair, analyst at Salomon Brothers in London.
Krupp planned to issue a statement later in the day.

The takeover could also face political hurdles as government officials fear another round of explosive protests just days after thousands of German miners marched on Bonn, blocking streets and disrupting government business to protest against cuts in subsidies to the coal industry.

The European Commission said it had not been notified by Germany's Federal Cartel Office of a Krupp-Thyssen merger, but European Union sources said a merger of the two steel giants would surely be reviewed by the EU.
The takeover attempt marks the second time in six years that Cromme, a smooth-operating Harvard Business School graduate, has shunned German aversions to hostile takeovers.
Instead, most mergers are carefully orchestrated by the bankers who sit on the boards of most German blue chip firms.
The mood was almost identical that seen during Krupp's 1991 surprise takeover of Hoesch AG.
Following the bombshell announcement that Krupp was poised to seize control of Hoesch, management and workers vowed to fight to retain their independence but it was all in vain.
Cromme had secretly amassed a sizeable stake in his rival and convinced a majority of the remaining shareholders to back the merger.
